slot.brief: Give volumes and molarities of an acid and a base (with clear stoichiometry like HCl vs NaOH) and ask for the volume of one needed for complete neutralisation of the other.

stem: What volume of $0.15\ \text{M}\ \text{NaOH}$ solution is required to completely neutralise $60\ \text{mL}$ of $0.10\ \text{M}\ \text{HCl}$ solution?

verdicts.working: HCl + NaOH → NaCl + H2O (1:1). Moles HCl = 0.060 L × 0.10 M = 0.006 mol. V(NaOH) = 0.006/0.15 = 0.040 L = 40 mL.

working:
The balanced chemical equation for the neutralisation reaction is:
$$\text{HCl} + \text{NaOH} \rightarrow \text{NaCl} + \text{H}_2\text{O}$$

The stoichiometric ratio of $\text{HCl}$ to $\text{NaOH}$ is $1 : 1$.

Calculate the millimoles of $\text{HCl}$ present:
$$\text{Millimoles of } \text{HCl} = M_1 \times V_1 = 0.10\ \text{M} \times 60\ \text{mL} = 6.0\ \text{mmol}$$

For complete neutralisation, the millimoles of $\text{NaOH}$ must equal the millimoles of $\text{HCl}$:
$$M_2 \times V_2 = 6.0\ \text{mmol}$$
$$0.15\ \text{M} \times V_2 = 6.0\ \text{mmol}$$
$$V_2 = \dfrac{6.0}{0.15} = 40\ \text{mL}$$

Independent check: HCl + NaOH → NaCl + H2O (1:1). Moles HCl = 0.060 L × 0.10 M = 0.006 mol. V(NaOH) = 0.006/0.15 = 0.040 L = 40 mL.
